newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia PM pledges foreign investment push.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia PM pledges foreign investment push.

text.p: Mongolia's prime minister said on Wednesday his government was pushing ahead with plans to promote the private sector and make the landlocked nation more attractive to foreign investors.
"Opening our country to private foreign investment is one of the highest priorities of my government," Prime Minister Mendsaikhany Enkhsaikhan told an investment conference.
"We are confident that we will succeed in developing a viable private sector-led economy in Mongolia," said the leader of Mongolia's 10-month-old reformist government.

Enkhsaikhan's reformist forces upset the former communists in parliamentary elections last year, but voters gave a strong mandate to the former communist candidate in the presidential elections last month.

The presidency is largely a figurehead but the victory of Natsagiin Bagabandi, candidate of the former communist party, has led some Western diplomats in Ulan Bator to question the future of economic reforms.

Voters in this vast but remote country wedged between Russia and China appeared to have rejected steep price rises and growing unemployment that have accompanied free market policies in the nation's rush to abandon economic central planning.

The prime minister told business officials, largely from the mining and energy sectors, that parliament was discussing a new minerals law and a new investment promotion law would be drafted in future.
"Our new investment promotion law will slash the procedures required for opening a business to a bare minimum," Enkhsaikhan said.
Only a handful of sectors, including finance, would require special permission to set up in Mongolia. He did not give details of the minerals law.
Mongolia also plans to relax border controls, permitting many foreigners to obtain visas on arrival as of July 1.

A new wave of privatisations was also being drawn up, and foreigners would be allowed to participate in auctions that would sell off most state enterprises to the private sector over the next 18 months, the prime minister said.
Mongolia was also planning to turn its sales tax into a value-added tax.
That would be twinned with a reduction in business income tax to 30 percent as of next year. Some businesses now pay 40 percent.
Mongolia had already abolished almost all import tariffs on May 1 this year.
"We want the flow of goods, capital, technology and people between Mongolia and the rest of the world to be as smooth as possible," the prime minister said.
President-elect Bagabandi, also attending the conference, said he would support the reforms.
"As president, I will work for keeping the political situation stable and support the transition to democracy and a market economy," he said.
